questions.text: According to Techriz, what is the primary function of a demand level?
options: To sponsor price movement downward and prevent further upward movement.
To sponsor price movement upward and prevent further downward movement.
To identify every order block within a market structure.
To ensure price retraces to the equilibrium level before every move.

questions.text: Which statement best describes a supply level in the lesson?
options: A level that supports price from moving further downward and encourages bullish continuation.
A level that represents only the last bullish candle before a bearish break of structure.
A level that prevents further upward movement and sponsors price movement downward.
A level that must always be completely mitigated before price can fall.

questions.text: How does Techriz distinguish demand and supply from points of interest (POIs)?
options: Demand and supply are individual candles, while POIs are entire market trends.
Demand and supply describe broader zones, while POIs are specific areas or formations within those zones.
Demand and supply are used only in uptrends, while POIs are used only in downtrends.
Demand and supply and POIs mean exactly the same thing.

questions.text: According to Techriz, which market conditions are associated with the formation of demand and supply?
options: Demand forms in a downtrend, while supply forms in an uptrend.
Both demand and supply form exclusively during sideways markets.
Demand and supply form only after an equilibrium retracement.
Demand forms in an uptrend, while supply forms in a downtrend.

questions.text: In the lesson, what market behaviour indicates that demand is being formed?
options: Price makes impulsive moves upward, rejects lower lows, and breaks new highs.
Price repeatedly breaks new lows while rejecting old highs.
Price remains within a narrow range without breaking structure.
Price retraces below equilibrium without any bullish movement.

questions.text: According to Techriz, how is the full demand zone identified following an upward break?
options: It consists exclusively of the last bearish candle before the break.
It begins at the equilibrium midline and ends at the discount level.
It spans from the highest point before the break to the lowest point after the break.
It includes only the fair value gap created by the break.

questions.text: What does Techriz identify as the full supply zone following a bearish structural move?
options: Only the last bullish candle before price moves downward.
The entire zone extending from point A to point B in the described bearish move.
Only the area below the equilibrium midline.
The nearest unmitigated bullish order block.

questions.text: Which combination contains the two primary points of interest Techriz says he uses for trading in this lesson?
options: Rejection blocks and breaker blocks.
Equilibrium levels and inducement levels.
Internal range liquidity and change in state of delivery.
Order blocks and fair value gaps.

questions.text: Which of the following lists contains POIs that Techriz mentions can exist inside demand or supply zones?
options: Order blocks, fair value gaps, rejection blocks, and breaker blocks.
Trendlines, moving averages, RSI, and MACD.
Support levels, resistance levels, moving averages, and trend channels.
Point A, point B, equilibrium, and discount levels only.

questions.text: What does the equilibrium pricing rule described by Techriz suggest after price breaks above a level to establish demand?
options: Price must immediately continue upward without retracing.
Price must return to the exact origin of the move before continuing.
Price should retrace into the demand zone at least to equilibrium before pushing upward, according to the rule.
Price must first break below the demand zone before a buy can be considered.

questions.text: Which tools does Techriz mention for identifying the equilibrium level within a demand or supply zone?
options: The RSI and MACD indicators.
The Fibonacci retracement tool and the Gann box.
The volume profile and moving averages.
The trendline tool and stochastic oscillator.

questions.text: In Techriz’s explanation of bullish equilibrium pricing, which part of the demand zone is described as the most premium area to look for a potential buy?
options: The area above the highest point of the demand zone.
The area above the equilibrium midline, toward the highest point.
The exact point where price first breaks structure, regardless of its location.
The area from the equilibrium midline down to the discount level.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what is mitigation when discussing a point of interest such as an order block?
options: Price enters or taps the point of interest, uses it, and moves away, exhausting that area.
Price breaks a previous high or low to confirm a new trend.
Price reaches the equilibrium midline for the first time.
Price forms a new fair value gap without returning to it.

questions.text: What does Techriz say can happen when price revisits an order block that has already been mitigated?
options: It must reverse immediately because the order block remains fresh.
It automatically creates a new demand zone.
It may be treated as liquidity and used to induce price before moving upward, rather than serving as a fresh point of interest.
It invalidates every equilibrium level in the surrounding market.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what condition can invalidate the expectation of price respecting the equilibrium/discount area as described in the lesson?
options: The market has formed a new high or low.
There are no unmitigated points of interest remaining in the relevant zone.
Price has touched the equilibrium midline once.
The zone contains both demand and supply.

questions.text: What does Techriz mean when he says the entire demand zone can be fulfilled even if price has not mitigated an order block inside it?
options: The demand zone is valid only when every order block has been touched.
Price can tap the broader demand zone and move upward without reaching a specific POI inside it.
The demand zone becomes supply as soon as price moves upward.
Price must always reach the discount level before a demand zone can be fulfilled.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what is the role of internal range liquidity in the bearish supply-zone example?
options: It guarantees that price will reverse immediately upon entering supply.
It identifies the exact equilibrium midline within the supply zone.
It is what price seeks within the supply zone before a change in state of delivery (CISD) and a subsequent upward move.
It replaces the need to identify supply zones.

questions.text: In the bearish equilibrium pricing example, what does Techriz say traders should look for before expecting price to move downward?
options: Price should enter the supply area above the equilibrium midline, show a change in state of delivery (CISD), and then move downward.
Price must first break above the entire supply zone and establish a new uptrend.
Price should enter the demand zone below equilibrium and form a bullish order block.
Price must completely mitigate every supply POI before moving downward.

questions.text: How does Techriz describe the relationship between a point of interest and the broader demand or supply zone?
options: A POI must always occupy the entire demand or supply zone.
A POI is valid only when it lies outside the demand or supply zone.
A demand or supply zone can contain only one POI at a time.
Multiple POIs, such as order blocks and fair value gaps, can exist within the broader demand or supply zone.

questions.text: Which topic does Techriz identify as the focus of the follow-up lessons after introducing demand and supply?
options: Risk management, trading psychology, and account management.
Points of interest, including order blocks, bullish and bearish order blocks, fair value gaps, and breaker blocks.
Fundamental analysis, economic news, and interest rates.
Liquidity sweeps, trade journaling, and position sizing.

questions.text: What does Techriz say should guide a trader’s bias when identifying and trading this order block pattern?
options: The number of candles in the pattern.
The market structure and the direction of price.
The size of the previous candle’s body alone.
The timeframe on which the pattern first appears.

questions.text: On which timeframes does Techriz recommend primarily considering this order block pattern to reduce market noise?
options: Only the M1 and M5 timeframes.
Only the M15 timeframe.
Typically H4 and above, while noting that H1 and above can also be considered.
Exclusively the daily timeframe, with no exceptions.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what candlestick pattern appears before the next candle engulfs it in this particular order block setup?
options: A green inverse pin bar, also described as an inverse hammer.
A bearish engulfing candle followed by a doji.
A bullish hammer followed by a smaller bearish candle.
Two consecutive candles with identical bodies.

questions.text: What does the upper wick of the inverse pin bar indicate in Techriz’s explanation?
options: Buyers have maintained complete control throughout the candle.
Price has successfully broken above the previous high.
The candle has no directional significance.
Sellers have pushed price down from its high, showing rejection of buying pressure.

questions.text: What makes this particular order block pattern different from the bearish interpretation someone might initially give to the inverse pin bar?
options: The inverse pin bar must always be followed by a doji.
The next candle engulfs the rejection candle, showing that buyers have regained strength.
The next candle must close below the rejection candle’s low.
Price must immediately reverse downward after the inverse pin bar forms.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what is the significance of the next candle completely engulfing the inverse pin bar?
options: It confirms that the market must continue selling.
It proves that every nearby supply zone has been invalidated.
It indicates that buyers have regained strength and closed above the rejection wick.
It means the market has entered a sideways range.

questions.text: In the bullish setup described by Techriz, where does he identify the potential entry area?
options: Anywhere within the rejection wick of the inverse pin bar.
Only at the close of the candle that created the original rejection.
At the previous swing low, regardless of the pattern’s location.
Only after price has moved completely beyond the entire pattern and never returned.

questions.text: Where does Techriz typically place the stop loss for the bullish order block setup?
options: Above the high of the engulfing candle.
At the equilibrium midpoint of the entire trend.
Exactly at the entry price.
Below the identified pattern’s low.

questions.text: What does Techriz recommend considering before treating this order block as a strong trading opportunity?
options: Whether the pattern appears on every timeframe simultaneously.
Whether the pattern aligns with the market’s structure and the trader’s bias.
Whether the previous candle has a larger body than every candle nearby.
Whether price has already reached the final target.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what can a trader do instead of entering the setup immediately without additional confirmation?
options: Ignore the order block and enter in the opposite direction.
Move the stop loss to the entry price before entering the trade.
Wait for confirmation within the order block area before taking the trade.
Switch to a lower timeframe and disregard the broader market structure.

questions.text: In Techriz’s gold example, what happened when price returned to the area containing the fair value gap and the identified order block?
options: Price immediately broke downward and continued selling.
Price remained inside the area without making a significant move.
Price invalidated the entire bullish market structure.
Price entered the area, formed the inverse pin bar pattern, and the next candle closed above it before the subsequent bullish move.

questions.text: Why does Techriz consider the order block in his gold example significant?
options: It was the last point of contact before a substantial breakout and upward movement.
It was the first candle of the entire trading session.
It formed after price had already completed the entire upward move.
It appeared without any relationship to a fair value gap or market structure.

questions.text: In the gold example, what happened before the inverse pin bar appeared at the identified area?
options: Price broke above the entire supply zone and never retraced.
Price took liquidity and mitigated the identified support level.
Price formed a new low without interacting with any previous level.
Price moved directly to its target without revisiting a point of interest.

questions.text: According to Techriz, why might traders initially misinterpret the inverse pin bar at a support or point-of-interest area?
options: They assume every inverse pin bar signals an immediate bullish reversal.
They believe the candle has no relationship to buying or selling pressure.
They may interpret the rejection wick as evidence that selling will continue, before the subsequent candle shows strong buying pressure.
They assume the pattern can occur only in a sideways market.

questions.text: What does Techriz say can make the identified entry more precise than entering at a more obvious nearby level?
options: Using the order block area can provide a tighter risk-to-reward ratio.
Increasing the stop loss until it covers the entire trading session.
Entering before the rejection candle has closed.
Ignoring the location of the stop loss when calculating risk.

questions.text: In Techriz’s explanation, what can a break of structure after price bounces from a point of interest indicate?
options: That the market must reverse in the opposite direction.
That the point of interest can no longer be used.
That price will remain within the same range indefinitely.
It can serve as confirmation that price may continue moving in the direction of the bounce.

questions.text: Which statement best reflects Techriz’s explanation of old lows and liquidity in his USD/JPY example?
options: Old lows cannot act as liquidity pools once price has moved away from them.
Old lows can serve as liquidity pools, and price taking an old low can precede the order block pattern he describes.
Old lows are always the correct entry for every bullish order block.
Taking an old low automatically confirms that the market will continue downward.

questions.text: What does Techriz demonstrate with his USD/JPY examples?
options: The pattern works only on gold and should not be considered on other instruments.
The pattern is useful only when price moves downward.
The pattern can occur on USD/JPY as well, where strong buying can overcome a candle that initially appears bearish.
The pattern works only when there is no fair value gap nearby.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about the order block pattern when it appears on the daily timeframe and supports an upward move?
options: It may support a substantial upward continuation, with price potentially providing further opportunities to enter as it rises.
It should always be traded against the existing market structure.
It is less significant than the same pattern on every lower timeframe.
It guarantees that price will rise continuously without any retracement.

questions.text: Which statement correctly summarizes Techriz’s position on the direction in which this order block pattern can be used?
options: It is strictly a bullish pattern and cannot be applied to selling.
It can be used only when gold is trending upward.
It is valid only on the daily timeframe and only for buy entries.
The pattern can also be applied to sell trades, not just buy trades.

questions.text: What does FVG stand for, according to Techriz?
options: Fair Volume Gradient
Fair Value Gap
Fixed Value Guide
Future Volume Gap

questions.text: According to Techriz, how many candles make up a fair value gap?
options: Two candles
Four candles
Three candles
Five candles

questions.text: When identifying a fair value gap using the three-candle model, which area does Techriz emphasize?
options: The space between the wicks of the first and third candles.
The distance between the opening prices of the first and second candles.
The body of the middle candle alone.
The distance between the closing prices of the second and third candles.

questions.text: How does Techriz describe the market condition represented by a fair value gap?
options: A period in which price remains completely balanced.
A zone where price must reverse immediately.
A formation that occurs only when the market is moving sideways.
An imbalance in price action involving the three-candle formation.

questions.text: Why does Techriz describe fair value gaps as “price magnets”?
options: They prevent price from making new highs or lows.
They represent imbalances that price may return to so the inefficient price action can be rebalanced.
They guarantee a reversal whenever price reaches them.
They eliminate the need to identify other points of interest.

questions.text: Which two types of price action does Techriz say the market continually moves between?
options: Bullish and bearish candlesticks only.
Breakouts and stop losses.
Balanced or efficient price action, and the rebalancing of inefficient price action.
Support and resistance without any imbalances.

questions.text: Which role does Techriz assign to fair value gaps in a continuation setup?
options: They can provide areas from which price continues in the established direction.
They must always reverse the existing trend.
They replace the need to identify the prevailing trend.
They guarantee that price will return to the original order block.

questions.text: According to Techriz, how can a fair value gap help when evaluating a reversal order block?
options: It automatically invalidates every order block nearby.
It confirms a reversal regardless of the surrounding price action.
It means the trader no longer needs confirmation.
It can help validate the order block as part of the reversal setup.

questions.text: In Techriz’s explanation, what can make a setup involving an unmitigated point of interest more compelling?
options: Having no identifiable liquidity near the point of interest.
Having a fair value gap close to the unmitigated point of interest, alongside the other elements of the setup.
Entering before the point of interest has been reached.
Ignoring the market structure and relying only on the fair value gap.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about using a fair value gap as a trading opportunity without knowing how to identify it on a chart?
options: A trader can always identify it by looking at the candle colours alone.
Drawing the formation is unnecessary, even without an indicator.
A trader needs to understand how to identify or draw the fair value gap to trade it properly.
Fair value gaps can be traded only when a broker identifies them.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what happens when a candle’s wick penetrates more than 50% of the relevant candle’s range in the example he discusses?
options: The formation automatically becomes a weekly fair value gap.
The formation becomes a confirmed reversal setup.
The fair value gap becomes stronger because price has penetrated further into it.
It fails the FVG condition he describes, and he identifies the area as another block instead.

questions.text: What does Techriz recommend doing with fair value gaps when the market is in a retracement profile, rather than a continuation profile?
options: Ignore the fair value gaps in that retracement profile, according to his explanation.
Trade every fair value gap in the direction of the retracement.
Use fair value gaps as the only confirmation for entry.
Assume every retracement will immediately reverse.

questions.text: In the continuation example, what did price do when it reached the fair value gap?
options: It broke through the zone and continued downward without reacting.
It ignored the fair value gap and returned to the previous order block.
It entered the fair value gap and rejected upward, continuing the move.
It remained inside the fair value gap until the trend ended.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about price continuing to move after a trend shift and confirmation have been established?
options: Price must return to the original order block for every continuation.
Price can continue to buy from fair value gaps as the established bullish move progresses.
Price can no longer react to fair value gaps once a shift occurs.
Every fair value gap formed after a shift should be treated as a reversal.

questions.text: What does Techriz recommend when the three candles in a potential fair value gap do not have the wicks needed for the formation he describes?
options: Treat the formation as a valid fair value gap regardless.
Use the middle candle’s body as a substitute for the missing wicks.
Enter immediately if the candles are moving in the same direction.
Ignore that potential fair value gap.

questions.text: According to Techriz, which timeframes does he recommend primarily considering when trading fair value gaps?
options: M30 and above, or H1 and above.
M1 and M5 only.
M5 and M15 exclusively.
Only the monthly timeframe.

questions.text: How does Techriz describe the role of a fair value gap on the weekly timeframe?
options: It can be used only for continuation, never reversal.
It must be ignored because weekly charts contain too much information.
It has the potential to cause a reversal in price.
It automatically confirms a reversal without any further steps.

questions.text: What does Techriz insist traders should do when price reaches a fair value gap that appears relevant to their setup?
options: Enter immediately because price has reached the zone.
Wait for additional confirmation before entering the trade.
Remove the fair value gap from the chart.
Move the stop loss to the opposite side of the entire trend.

questions.text: Why does Techriz move from a higher timeframe to lower timeframes when examining a trading opportunity?
options: To replace the higher-timeframe market structure entirely.
To find more indicators to place on the chart.
To make every entry depend on the M1 timeframe.
To refine the entry and identify a more precise area where price reacted.

questions.text: Which sequence best reflects Techriz’s approach when he cannot find the information or confirmation he needs on a higher timeframe?
options: Step down through timeframes, such as from the daily to H4 and then H1, until the setup can be assessed more clearly.
Abandon the higher-timeframe analysis and enter immediately.
Switch exclusively to M5 and ignore all other timeframes.
Increase the stop loss until the trade becomes valid.

questions.text: In Techriz’s example involving a higher-timeframe demand zone, what did his lower-timeframe analysis help him identify?
options: A reason to discard the demand zone completely.
A guarantee that price would never retrace again.
A more precise order block within the broader area where price had reacted.
A reason to enter without considering the stop loss.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about fair value gaps that have already been mitigated?
options: They should be used repeatedly for every subsequent entry.
They should no longer be used once they have been mitigated.
They automatically become valid reversal order blocks.
They must always be redrawn on the same timeframe.

questions.text: In Techriz’s gold example, what does he observe about many of the continuation moves during the strong bullish movement?
options: They all begin at the same daily order block.
They occur only after price returns to the bottom of the entire range.
They consistently require price to revisit every previous order block.
Many of the continuation moves react from fair value gaps rather than returning to the previous order blocks.

questions.text: When explaining how to place orders around a fair value gap, what does Techriz say about stop-loss placement in relation to a nearby order block?
options: The stop loss can be placed below the order block or below the fair value gap, depending on the setup he describes.
The stop loss must always be placed above the fair value gap.
The stop loss must be placed exactly at the fair value gap’s midpoint.
The stop loss is unnecessary when price enters a fair value gap.

questions.text: What does Techriz recommend using a fair value gap indicator for, in addition to making the formations easier to identify?
options: Predicting every market reversal without further analysis.
Replacing the need to understand order blocks and market structure.
Helping identify fair value gaps across timeframes and validating a point of interest when the surrounding setup supports it.
Automatically opening and closing trades without trader confirmation.

questions.text: What does Techriz say is the logic behind a Quasimodo pattern?
options: Price forms a perfect head and shoulders at every high.
Price follows textbook higher highs and higher lows with no sweeps.
A valid block is taken out, price reclaims that zone, and price then returns to use that block.
Price breaks a trendline and never comes back to it.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what does it mean for price to “reclaim” a level?
options: Price climbs back above the level and closes above it.
Price touches the level with a wick only.
Price moves sideways beneath the level for several candles.
Price breaks the level and keeps going without returning.

questions.text: Techriz says people call this pattern many names. Which name does he call the general one?
options: Turtle soup
Engineered liquidity
Breakout block
Reclaim block

questions.text: How does Techriz describe a reclaim block in the simplest terms?
options: A block formed for the first time after a break of structure.
A block that was previously violated, which price then came back to reclaim.
A block that price has never touched.
A fair value gap formed by three candles.

questions.text: What is the difference between a QMR and a QMC, according to Techriz?
options: QMR is used only on lower timeframes, while QMC is used only on higher timeframes.
QMR is used only for buys, while QMC is used only for sells.
QMR is a reclaim block at a point of reversal, while QMC is a reclaim block on a continuation leg.
QMR needs a fair value gap, while QMC does not.

questions.text: What does Techriz say a QMC is a great way to do when you are confident a trade will reach its potential high or low?
options: Add more positions to maximize the trade.
Close the whole trade early.
Reverse the position at once.
Remove the stop loss.

questions.text: Why does Techriz tell traders to delete the textbook picture of how price moves?
options: Because higher highs and higher lows no longer exist.
Because the market does not react in that smooth way, and price sweeps levels before reaching new ground.
Because only lower timeframes matter.
Because indicators have replaced market structure.

questions.text: What does Techriz say price must do before it goes to the new side?
options: Form a fair value gap on every timeframe.
Retrace to the equilibrium of the whole range.
Close beyond the previous high without retracing.
Take some form of liquidity, such as sweeping a level.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what most times happens to a trader’s first entry at an obvious reversal point?
options: It gets swept, like engineered liquidity, before price reclaims the level.
It runs straight to target without any pullback.
It never gets touched again.
It is valid only on the weekly timeframe.

questions.text: What does Techriz say it tells a trader when price reclaims the level after stopping them out?
options: The trade idea is invalid and should be abandoned.
The trader should flip direction immediately.
The original directional bias is still correct, so they can look for their earlier entry or a higher-timeframe entry.
The trader should wait for a new market structure to form on the weekly timeframe.

questions.text: What does Techriz say price tends to do at highs that still have liquidity on them before a reversal?
options: It never touches those highs.
It takes the liquidity off the high, then retraces back and closes inside.
It breaks above and stays above permanently.
It stays flat until the next session.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about the timeframes on which this pattern can be found?
options: Only on the one-minute timeframe.
Only on the daily timeframe.
Only on the H4 timeframe.
It is not timeframe specific; the trader just needs to understand the trend and flow with it.

questions.text: In Techriz’s one-day chart example, what happens after the traders who sold on the change in state of delivery (CSD) get stopped out?
options: Price reclaims the level, then returns to the same area and drops, which he calls a Quasimodo reversal.
Price continues upward without ever returning.
Price forms a double top and ranges for weeks.
Price creates a new fair value gap and the trend ends.

questions.text: Where does Techriz say the major invalidation point (stop loss) is best placed in the one-day sell example?
options: Right below the reclaim block, because it gives the biggest reward.
At the entry price.
Above the high, since placing it tighter is not recommended even though it would show a bigger reward.
Beyond the external low.

questions.text: Why does Techriz say a trader who picked the fair value gap in his higher-timeframe bullish example would have missed the entry?
options: Because fair value gaps never form after a sweep.
Because price used the reclaim block instead, and only that block guaranteed getting the entry.
Because price never retraced at all.
Because the fair value gap formed on the weekly timeframe.

questions.text: Why does Techriz say holding the one-day timeframe examples is demanding?
options: Because spreads widen overnight.
Because they need constant lower-timeframe monitoring.
Because the pattern repeats every hour.
Because each candle is a day, so the trader may sit on the trade for a very long time.

questions.text: In Techriz’s H4 example, why did many traders miss the entry?
options: They expected price to return to the bullish engulfing candle, but price bounced from the reclaimed block instead.
They entered before the low was swept.
They ignored the sweep of the low.
Their stop loss was too wide.

questions.text: Where does Techriz stress that these patterns happen?
options: In the middle of ranging markets.
At points of reversal.
Only after news releases.
Only at the weekly open.

questions.text: In Techriz’s sell example, what targets does he describe?
options: A single target at the equilibrium of the range.
The first target is the nearby highs, and the last target is the external high.
The first target is the nearby lows, and the last target is the external low.
No targets, because the trade is held without a plan.

questions.text: How does Techriz suggest using timeframes to reduce risk when trading these patterns?
options: Trade only on the one-minute chart.
Ignore higher timeframes completely.
Always wait for the weekly candle to close before acting.
Find them on higher timeframes where reversals are expected, then drop to lower timeframes for confirmation.

questions.text: According to Techriz, what is the key thing that decides the direction of price?
options: Candlestick colour
Market structure
The news calendar
The trading session

questions.text: What does Techriz say about a trader who does not know the direction of price?
options: They can rely on indicators alone to win.
They only need a tight stop loss to win.
They will win on lower timeframes only.
They cannot have any winning trade.

questions.text: How does Techriz define market structure?
options: What is happening on a zoomed-out perspective of the chart, describing the behaviour of price.
The pattern made by the body and wick of a single candlestick.
The exact order blocks inside each candle.
The news events that move price.

questions.text: Which three things does Techriz say we talk about under market structure?
options: Candles, wicks, and bodies
Support, resistance, and indicators
Trends, profiles, and shifts
Highs, lows, and ranges

questions.text: How does Techriz define a trend?
options: The speed at which candles form.
The direction the market is currently moving in.
The distance between a high and a low.
A zone where price always reverses.

questions.text: What does an uptrend create, according to Techriz?
options: Higher highs and higher lows
Lower highs and lower lows
Equal highs and equal lows
Highs only, with no lows

questions.text: How does Techriz describe a downtrend?
options: Higher highs that keep forming.
A range with no direction.
One low followed by a long consolidation.
Lower lows and lower highs, each below the previous one.

questions.text: How does Techriz describe a ranging market?
options: It makes higher highs and higher lows.
It moves down with lower lows.
It moves sideways, also called consolidation or accumulation, without higher highs and lows or lower lows and highs.
It breaks out in a straight line.

questions.text: What rule does Techriz give for sustaining an uptrend?
options: A high must form a low above the previous high.
A low forms a new high above the previous one, and a high forms a low that does not go below the previous low.
A low must break below the previous low every time.
Highs and lows must always be the same size.

questions.text: If a swing trader checks market structure on the daily, which timeframe does Techriz give as an example of minor structure?
options: H4
Weekly
Monthly
Yearly

questions.text: What do the minor trends inside a major trend do, according to Techriz?
options: They replace the higher-timeframe trend.
They cancel out the major trend.
They only appear on the weekly timeframe.
They deliver price to where the higher timeframe wants it to go.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about the end of a trend?
options: It is always a ranging market.
It is a bigger version of the same trend.
It is the beginning of a new one.
It is a signal to stop trading.

questions.text: When a downtrend ends, what does Techriz say about the trend that forms next?
options: A new trend forms, but you cannot say for sure whether it is an uptrend or a ranging market.
It always becomes an uptrend.
It always becomes a ranging market.
Nothing forms until the weekly close.

questions.text: What does Techriz say about the moves inside the bigger structure, which he calls internal structure?
options: They cannot be traded.
They are tradable, and he traded them himself.
They must always be ignored.
They matter only on the weekly timeframe.

questions.text: What is a break of structure (BOS) responsible for, according to Techriz?
options: Changing the trend to a different one.
Marking out a ranging market.
Ending the trend.
Continuing price in the same direction.

questions.text: What is a change of character responsible for, according to Techriz?
options: Continuing price in the same direction.
Creating a ranging market.
Changing the trend to a different one.
Mitigating every point of interest.

questions.text: When does Techriz say a break of structure has happened?
options: Price successfully closes above a previous high or low, using a body close.
Price touches a previous high with a wick only.
Price reaches the equilibrium of the range.
Price returns to a point of interest.

questions.text: In an uptrend, what does Techriz say the protected level is?
options: The higher highs
The higher lows
The equal highs
The starting candle

options: Price makes a new high.
Price wicks briefly into a high.
Price retraces to a point of interest.
Price breaks below the protected higher low and closes below it.

questions.text: After a change of character, what does Techriz teach his students to wait for?
options: A new fair value gap.
A news release.
A break of structure in the new direction as confirmation, before looking for unmitigated points of interest.
A second change of character.

options: Reduced momentum, equilibrium shift, and liquidity grab

Failure swing, expansion break, and equal highs

Price breaks highs with ever-increasing momentum.
Price stays inside a range for weeks.
Price makes a new high on every candle.

Reduced momentum
A simple range break
Failure swing

questions.text: How does Techriz describe an expansion break?
options: A slow, progressive break over many candles that is the most effective signal.
A return of price to the range.
One or two long candles, often sponsored by news or high volume, that break the low; he considers it the least effective and rarely uses it.
